author: Pierre Bertaux
title: Was Hölderlin Mentally III
role_in_project: Hölderlin historical/archival critique
notes: Reflections describes Bertaux as casting serious doubt on conventional psychiatric accounts and emphasizing political, biographical, and archival context.
view_of_madness: contested diagnosis; behavior recontextualized historically and biographically
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Resists psychiatric reduction; reconstructs politics, grief, family circumstances, and institutional events around Hölderlin.
difference_from_current_thesis: Revisionist emphasis is on whether apparent pathology has been misconstrued and on political/biographical explanations; cumulative corrosion across heterogeneous ordinary relations is not the organizing concept.

author: Osamu Muramoto
title: Retrospective diagnosis of a famous historical figure: ontological, epistemic, and ethical considerations
publication: Philosophy, Ethics, and Humanities in Medicine
role_in_project: Conceptual literature on retrospective diagnosis
notes: Used for ontological, epistemic, and ethical problems of retrospective diagnosis.
primary_interpretive_frame: Ethics and epistemology of retrospective diagnosis
view_of_madness: retrospective diagnosis treated as ontologically, epistemically, and ethically problematic
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Supports caution about retrospective psychiatric certainty and interpretive authority.
difference_from_current_thesis: Does not reconstruct Hölderlin or theorize cumulative institutional/interpersonal corrosion.

author: G. von Bassermann-Jordan
title: “Wenn dunkel mir ist der Sinn,/Den Kunst und Sinnen hat Schmerzen/Gekostet von Anbeginn” (“When Dark Are My Mind and Heart/Which Paid from the Beginning/In Grief for Thought and Art”): Hölderlin in the “Hölderlin Tower”—Contemporary and Modern Diagnoses of His Illness, and Literary (Self-)Therapy
role_in_project: Recent Hölderlin diagnostic literature
notes: 2025 article. Especially relevant for Autenrieth's coercive treatment model, likely coercive measures in Hölderlin's case, mercury treatment, humiliation, and the tower poems as possible self-therapy.
view_of_madness: schizophrenia treated as the best-supported modern diagnosis, but retrospective uncertainty is explicitly acknowledged
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Discusses forced transport, coercive treatment, mercury, humiliation, incomplete records, tower life, and the possibility that treatment was harmful.
difference_from_current_thesis: The article is organized around diagnosis and literary self-therapy; it does not make cumulative corrosion across heterogeneous ordinary relations the central explanatory problem.

author: Valentina Bizzari; Francesca Brencio
title: Psychiatric Diagnosis as a Political and Social Device: Epistemological and Historical Insights on the Role of Collective Emotions
role_in_project: Conceptual framework: diagnosis as epistemological, political, and social device
notes: Supports analysis of diagnosis as historically situated and theory-laden.
primary_interpretive_frame: Diagnosis as political, social, and epistemological device
view_of_madness: diagnosis as historically situated and theory-laden
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Shows how diagnosis can operate socially and politically rather than only medically.
difference_from_current_thesis: Not Hölderlin-specific and does not analyze cumulative effects on one life across heterogeneous relations.

author: Giovanni Stanghellini
title: Logics of Discovery II: Lessons from Poetry—Parataxis as a Method That Can Complement the Narrative Compulsion in Vogue in Contemporary Mental Health Care
role_in_project: Hölderlin, poetry, phenomenological psychiatry, and interpretive authority
notes: Reflections records the uncited claim that Hölderlin was 'probably schizophrenic' and uses it as an example of a diagnostic premise becoming self-authorizing.
view_of_madness: psychiatric premise retained while poetry supplements narrative understanding
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Treats poetry as a resource for understanding experiences that diagnostic narrative may flatten.
difference_from_current_thesis: Does not make ordinary institutional relations or cumulative corrosion the explanatory object.

author: George Ikkos; A. Morgan
title: Psychiatric poetics: mental healthcare and Giovanni Stanghellini’s ‘Logics of Discovery’
role_in_project: Recent psychiatric/phenomenological reception
notes: Reflections states that Ikkos & Morgan begin with the premise that Hölderlin experienced severe mental disorder and cite Ikkos & Stanghellini (2022) for schizophrenia.
primary_interpretive_frame: Contemporary psychiatric reception of poetic/phenomenological method
view_of_madness: severe mental disorder / schizophrenia largely presupposed
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Useful foil for how modern psychiatric writing can inherit diagnostic premises about Hölderlin.
difference_from_current_thesis: Does not reconstruct relational or institutional conditions of the life.

author: George Ikkos; Giovanni Stanghellini
title: Sensibility and schizophrenia: Wilhelm Waiblinger on Friedrich Hölderlin’s life, poetry and madness-psychiatry in literature
role_in_project: Hölderlin diagnostic genealogy / Waiblinger reception
notes: Reflections identifies this as the source cited by Ikkos & Morgan (2026) for the schizophrenia framing and notes its reliance on Waiblinger's 1830 memoir.
view_of_madness: schizophrenia framing linked to historical literary testimony
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Engages the historical construction of Hölderlin's madness through testimony and later psychiatry.
difference_from_current_thesis: Centers diagnostic genealogy rather than the cumulative effects of ordinary coercive and destabilizing relations.

author: R. Horowski
title: The “Madness” of Friedrich Hölderlin: an iatrogenic intoxication
role_in_project: Alternative medical interpretation of Hölderlin
notes: Reflections summarizes Horowski's argument that some later symptoms may be consistent with consequences of calomel poisoning.
view_of_madness: later symptoms potentially explained in part by treatment effects
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Makes institutional treatment itself a possible contributor to later impairment.
difference_from_current_thesis: Offers a relatively specific medical causal hypothesis rather than a plural longitudinal account of corrosive relations.

author: A. C. Adler
title: Giorgio Agamben. Hölderlin’s Madness: Chronicle of a Dwelling Life, 1806–1843 (The Italian List)
role_in_project: Reception of Agamben's non-psychiatric/philosophical interpretation
notes: Review discussed in Reflections as questioning Agamben's explanatory claim about Hölderlin honoring the diagnosis that saved him from arrest.
view_of_madness: diagnosis philosophically reinterpreted rather than accepted straightforwardly
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Questions a contemporary attempt to make Hölderlin's later life carry a larger philosophical-political meaning.
difference_from_current_thesis: Current thesis resists making the life an emblem and centers cumulative ordinary relations instead.

author: Jerome C. Wakefield
title: False positives in psychiatric diagnosis: implications for human freedom
role_in_project: Conceptual literature on diagnosis, freedom, and social consequences
notes: Used to frame the social ramifications and authority of psychiatric diagnosis.
view_of_madness: diagnostic error can have major social consequences
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Supports the claim that diagnostic judgments can materially alter a person's freedom and social position.
difference_from_current_thesis: Does not analyze cumulative institutional life or Hölderlin's biography.

author: U. Kistner
title: Foucault’s Hölderlin
role_in_project: Hölderlin philosophical/literary reception
notes: Citation recorded in Reflections; no further bibliographic detail supplied there.
view_of_madness: Hölderlin read through Foucault's madness/unreason problematic
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Directly addresses the Foucault–Hölderlin relation that the current paper critiques.
difference_from_current_thesis: Needs close reading; likely focuses on Foucault's philosophical use of Hölderlin rather than corrosive institutional life.

author: Eric J. Engstrom
title: Clinical Psychiatry in Imperial Germany: A History of Psychiatric Practice
publication: Cornell Studies in the History of Psychiatry / Cornell University Press
role_in_project: Historical framework: psychiatric professionalization and jurisdiction
notes: Reflections uses Engstrom for psychiatry's construction of professional jurisdiction, disciplinary institutions, observation, and scientific legitimacy.
primary_interpretive_frame: Professionalization and jurisdiction of German psychiatry
view_of_madness: psychiatric knowledge embedded in professional and institutional formation
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Provides historical mechanisms through which psychiatric institutions gained authority over persons.
difference_from_current_thesis: Macro/institutional history, not a longitudinal reconstruction of one life.

author: Cristina Hanganu-Bresch; Carol Berkenkotter
title: Diagnosing Madness: The Discursive Construction of the Psychiatric Patient, 1850–1920
role_in_project: Discursive framework: construction of psychiatric identities and diagnostic authority
notes: Used for diagnosis as textual persuasion and a negotiated medicolegal/social process.
view_of_madness: diagnostic identity produced through textual, medicolegal, and social practices
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Very close to the Foucauldian side of the paper: how institutions and discourse make a psychiatric subject.
difference_from_current_thesis: Current thesis shifts from subject-construction to cumulative human consequences across multiple kinds of relations.

author: Wendy Gonaver
title: The Peculiar Institution and the Making of Modern Psychiatry, 1840–1880
publication: The University of North Carolina Press
role_in_project: Historical framework: institutions, authority, race, and psychiatry
notes: Historical context for institutional authority in psychiatry.
primary_interpretive_frame: Institutional history of psychiatry, authority, and race
view_of_madness: psychiatric practice historically embedded in social hierarchy and institutional power
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Shows psychiatric institutions as social worlds whose authority has material and interpersonal consequences.
difference_from_current_thesis: Not Hölderlin-specific and not organized around cumulative corrosion of a singular life.

author: Roy Porter; David Wright
title: The Confinement of the Insane: International Perspectives, 1800–1965
role_in_project: Methodology/history of confinement and psychiatric records
notes: Reflections highlights its methodological caution about the entanglement of fact and fiction in psychiatric records.
primary_interpretive_frame: Comparative history of confinement and psychiatric records
view_of_madness: historically mediated through institutions and records
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Provides methodological caution about records and the lived effects of confinement.
difference_from_current_thesis: Broad comparative institutional history rather than a theory of cumulative relational/institutional corrosion.

author: Ann Goldberg
title: Sex, Religion, and the Making of Modern Madness: The Eberbach Asylum and German Society, 1815-1849
role_in_project: Historical framework: social meaning of behavior, asylum power, and diagnostic construction
notes: Used to show how behavior can be transformed from socially meaningful action into psychiatric symptomatology.
primary_interpretive_frame: Social history of asylum, gender, religion, and diagnostic meaning
view_of_madness: socially meaningful conduct can be transformed into psychiatric symptom
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Strong precedent for restoring social meaning and institutional context to behavior later treated as symptom.
difference_from_current_thesis: Does not focus on Hölderlin or on cumulative corrosion across a whole biography.

author: Philippe Pinel
title: A Treatise on Insanity (1801)
role_in_project: Historical psychiatric context
notes: Reflections lists G. Eghigian as editor and uses the text for observation, repeated examination, moral treatment, authority, and coercion.
primary_interpretive_frame: Early psychiatric theory and moral treatment
view_of_madness: historical psychiatric classification and treatment
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Primary historical context for examination, moral treatment, medical authority, and coercion.
difference_from_current_thesis: Primary contextual source, not a competing interpretation.

author: Johann Christian August Heinroth
role_in_project: Historical psychiatric context / concepts of mental illness
notes: Reflections discusses Heinroth's 1818 conception of mental illness as spiritual, moral, and existential but does not give a title.
view_of_madness: mental illness conceptualized in moral, spiritual, and existential terms
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Historical context showing that diagnostic meaning itself was heterogeneous.
difference_from_current_thesis: Primary contextual source, not a competing interpretation.

author: Frantz Fanon
title: The Wretched of the Earth
role_in_project: Political and philosophical critique of psychiatric interpretation
notes: Reflections also discusses 'The North African Syndrome' (1952), but does not provide a separate full citation for it.
primary_interpretive_frame: Colonial, political, and social production of psychic suffering
view_of_madness: psychic suffering cannot be detached from social and political conditions
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Strong methodological resonance: distress may be produced or intensified by coercive social worlds rather than residing solely inside the individual.
difference_from_current_thesis: Different historical and colonial context; should be used as resonance, not as a direct explanatory model for Hölderlin.

author: Wilhelm Waiblinger
title: Friedrich Hoelderlin's Life, Poetry and Madness
role_in_project: Foundational Hölderlin reception / diagnostic genealogy
notes: Title and date are recorded in Reflections in the discussion of Ikkos & Stanghellini (2022); publication details remain incomplete.
view_of_madness: madness presented through personal observation and literary narrative
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Foundational testimony about Hölderlin's later life and behavior.
difference_from_current_thesis: A primary reception source whose literary shaping is itself part of the diagnostic genealogy, not a competing contemporary theory.

author: Shane Weller
title: Literature and the Politics of Madness: On the Twentieth-Century Reception of Friedrich Hölderlin in France and Germany
role_in_project: Reception history: Foucault, Heidegger, Blanchot, Adorno, Lacoue-Labarthe, Badiou
notes: Central comparison source for how Hölderlin is repeatedly made exemplary within psychiatric, philosophical, aesthetic, and political interpretations.
primary_interpretive_frame: Reception history / critique of exemplary philosophical interpretation
view_of_madness: madness and unreason treated as contested interpretive categories within reception history
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Shows repeated conversion of Hölderlin into an interpretable emblem and questions the privilege accorded to madness and literature.
difference_from_current_thesis: Weller's endpoint is the uninterpretable sign; the current project returns to the historical person and the cumulative effects of ordinary social and institutional relations.

author: Ian Hacking
title: Déraison
role_in_project: Foucault publication history and changing role of déraison
notes: Tracks the fading of déraison from Foucault's framing and the abandonment of the idea of an underlying primitive purity of madness.
primary_interpretive_frame: Intellectual history of Foucault's concept of déraison
view_of_madness: distinguishes madness from unreason and emphasizes shifts in Foucault's own framing
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Helps delimit the early Foucauldian claim being criticized and shows that Foucault later moved away from some of its romantic assumptions.
difference_from_current_thesis: Does not propose a biographical or institutional alternative for Hölderlin.

author: Stuart Elden
title: Discipline, Health and Madness: Foucault's Le pouvoir psychiatrique
role_in_project: Later Foucault: psychiatric power, microphysics, tactics, bodies
notes: Elden presents Le pouvoir psychiatrique as an explicit rewriting of the latter part of Histoire de la folie. Three shifts: representations→power; violence→microphysics; institution/state apparatus→dispositions/tactics of power.
primary_interpretive_frame: Later Foucault: rewriting of History of Madness through psychiatric power, genealogy, and microphysics
view_of_madness: focus shifts from representations of madness to the power relations and practices that produce psychiatric knowledge
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Provides the strongest Foucauldian framework for dispersed, capillary relations of power acting on bodies, conduct, time, and institutional life.
difference_from_current_thesis: Foucault's object is the operation and rationality of power; the current project asks about the cumulative human consequences of heterogeneous relations across a life.

author: Gabriel Rockhill
title: Foucault, Genealogy, Counter-History
role_in_project: Alternative to streamlined genealogy; multidimensional counter-history
notes: Rockhill's positive alternative maps history as a multi-agential force field across time, space, and social stratification. Useful methodological comparator, but not a Hölderlin interpretation.
view_of_madness: not central
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Explicitly argues for constitutive multidimensionality, multiple agencies, social stratification, and conjunctural analysis against streamlined genealogical narratives.
difference_from_current_thesis: The current project is case-centered and does not assume that political struggle, class, or social stratification should organize the causal plurality revealed by a singular life.

author: Anthony Curtis Adler
title: Politics and Truth in Hölderlin: Hyperion and the Choreographic Project of Modernity
role_in_project: Recent political-philosophical interpretation of Hölderlin
notes: Priority source. Adler explicitly distinguishes world-historical revolution from 'life events' such as humiliations as a private tutor and the Susette relationship, but subsumes the life within a larger political-philosophical argument.
view_of_madness: institutionalization appears within a wider world-historical and political account rather than as the central diagnostic problem
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Uses many of the same ordinary pressures: tutoring humiliation, blocked vocation, mother-controlled patrimony, state debt through the Stift, Susette, politics, Sinclair, and institutionalization.
difference_from_current_thesis: Adler explicitly makes the French Revolution and the choreographic project of modernity the organizing world-historical horizon; the current thesis foregrounds ordinary heterogeneous relations and their cumulative corrosive effects without a single political master narrative.

author: Uwe Gonther; Jann E. Schlimme
title: Hölderlin und die Psychiatrie
publication: In Johann Kreuzer (ed.), Hölderlin-Handbuch: Leben – Werk – Wirkung, 2nd rev. ed., J.B. Metzler
role_in_project: Recent psychiatric-biographical reinterpretation of the tower years
notes: Handbook chapter now available. Authors stress restraint, source-based reconstruction, crisis/recovery, continuing limitations, healthy capacities, and active participation in tower life. Their endpoint is Entpsychiatrisierung, not 'corrosive institutional life'.
view_of_madness: severe crises in 1802 and 1806 cautiously described as psychotic experiences; rejects the myth of permanent 'mental darkness'
closest_overlap_with_current_thesis: Strongly emphasizes evidentiary modesty, sparse records, projection risk, difficult recovery, continued capacities, active shaping of life, and disturbance of communicative embeddedness in the social world.
difference_from_current_thesis: Gonther/Schlimme organize the account around psychotic crisis, recovery, and de-psychiatrization; they do not make cumulative corrosion across family, employment, political, medical, and interpersonal relations the central longitudinal concept.
